chapter_theme: Kurinji: the invocation to the elephant god (0), then the hill lovers' secret love, the friend's pleas to the man not to forget and to marry (1, 5, 7, 11), the girl's trust in his pledge (2, 4, 8, 9, 14), her care for him on the night path (10), the friend shielding her from the mother and the velan's rite (6, 12), and the coming that ends the mother's harrying (13).

0.reading: The invocation asks that the elephant born of the god with the eye in his forehead, he of the skull, of the whole universe, of the root of things and of the fair dark throat, bring every purpose we hold sweetly to its end and grant us all the arts.
0.nuance: The elephant god is never named; he is known only as the offspring (ஈன்ற களிறு) of Siva, who is drawn by four epithets ending in -த்தான். The prayer asks for success in what one intends and for learning, the two things a poet beginning a book needs.

thinai_evidence.note: praise and prayer to a god, the கடவுள் வாழ்த்து placed under paadaan

1.reading: The friend tells the lord of the forest land, whose spreading slopes see the yak and the gaur graze on the green-eared millet twined with avarai beans, not to forget that she stood as the raft between him and the girl of bright jewels.
1.nuance: The friend claims her own part: the love was crossed to on her as on a raft, so forgetting the girl would also be forgetting the one who carried him. The beasts eating a guarded millet field invite a hidden reading of the man taking what is watched over, but only one correspondence can be named, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field of the slopes and its raiding hill beasts

comparisons.tenor: the friend herself, the raft that carried him across to the girl

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

2.reading: The girl says that she trusted the assurance given by the lord of the hills, where a troop of black-faced langurs leaps on the boulder of the village common, thought it good and was set at rest; his grace, she says, is one and the same from first to last.
2.nuance: Three forms of one root, தெளித்த, தெளிவினை, தெளிந்தேன், make the verse a small study of trust: he made her clear, she weighed it (தேறி) and then was clear. The last line is the doubtful one; it is read here as saying his kindness is the same throughout.

thinai_evidence.note: langurs on the boulders of the hill country

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

3.reading: The girl says they cannot part from the lord of the lovely mountain, where a female monkey, having eaten the sweet ripe fruit of the jackfruit on the common, strokes the udder of a wild cow, and the cow, as glad as with her own calf, lets her milk flow.
3.nuance: The milk is not taken but given: the cow lets it down (சுரக்கும்) because the touch feels like her calf's, so tenderness flows across kinds.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey and the wild cow of the hill slopes

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; it could also be the friend telling the man that they (the girl and she) will not part from him

iraicchi.act: the wild cow, stroked by the monkey as if by her calf, gladly lets her milk flow to it
iraicchi.sense: a heart once touched with tenderness gives itself and cannot be withdrawn, so the girl cannot part from the man who has won her

4.reading: The girl says her heart tells her that, as the friendship of the worthy stands firm without decay, grows into strength and keeps yielding good afterwards, so the friendship of the lord of the mountain, with its groves bright with pools, will shine with goodness and never weaken.
4.nuance: The first two lines are a maxim of the ethics books, set down whole before the love situation; the girl's trust rests on ranking her lover among the சான்றவர், and it is her heart, not her friend, that makes the argument.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain land and its groves

comparisons.tenor: the mountain lord's bond with her, set beside the friendship of the worthy

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

5.reading: The friend tells the lord of the good mountain, whose dense groves smell of the vengai's golden clusters, not to forget that the girl of bright jewels has no medicine but him to keep her sweet life, and asks whether he will not give it out of kindness.
5.nuance: Line 2 repeats verse 1's மறவல் வயங்கிழைக்கு, so the friend's plea has a refrain. The gift she asks for is named by the Kural's word for regard toward one's own, கண்ணோட்டம், making his return a duty of kindness rather than a favour.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowering vengai of the mountain groves

comparisons.tenor: the man himself, the only medicine that can hold up her life

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

6.reading: The friend tells the mother not to rage, since the girl is not at fault: her eyes turned red because she bathed again and again in the waterfall that came down mixed with honey in the red, swollen water of the forest stream.
6.nuance: The excuse is precise enough to be believed: red flood water, honey in the stream, long bathing. What reddened the eyes is left unsaid, and the friend's defence is itself the sign that the girl has been weeping for her lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest stream and hill waterfall

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

7.reading: The friend asks the lord of the fragrant cool groves, where the cool water of a fragrant spring brims over and the sweet ripe fruit of the mango on which pepper vine climbs falls into it, whether any folly can stand where knowledge stands.
7.nuance: The rebuke is a compliment turned against him: he is wise, so his delay must be the one folly wisdom cannot hold. The ripe fruit falling into the brimming spring has been read as the girl ready for marriage; it is one match of mood only, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the spring, pepper vine and mango of the hill groves

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; the question presses him to act as his knowledge requires, that is, to marry

8.reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the land of falling waterfalls, where in the burnt clearing the boar has ploughed a male monkey buries mature plantains to ripen and then rests, has given her his pledge, and that pledge is the staff her heart leans on.
8.nuance: The monkey's stored fruit and the girl's stored promise both wait to ripen; the comfort is in having put something by.

thinai_evidence.note: the burnt hill clearing, the boar and the monkey

comparisons.tenor: his pledge, the staff her heart leans on

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

iraicchi.act: the male monkey buries unripe plantains in the ploughed clearing to let them ripen and then rests at ease
iraicchi.sense: the man has laid his pledge by as the monkey lays by its fruit, so she can rest on it until it ripens into marriage

9.reading: The bond with the mountain lord of the bee-loud groves, where a great-trunked dark bull elephant eats hill paddy and sleeps in the green-leaved shade of the black-stemmed kadamba grove, gives safety to those who join with it.
9.nuance: ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து is the didactic books' word for lasting protection; here it is said of a lover's bond.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant, hill paddy and kadamba grove of the mountain

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; the general statement could equally be the friend's reassurance to the girl

iraicchi.act: the elephant, fed, lies down to sleep without fear in the shade of the grove
iraicchi.sense: as the elephant sleeps secure in the grove's shade, the woman joined to this man may rest without fear

10.reading: The girl tells her friend that she has one want: to keep safe a life that is dear to her, so tell the lord of the long groves where snakes move that he must not come to their house by night.
10.nuance: The refusal is made out of care: the danger is to him on the snake path, and asking him to stop coming is how she protects him. அரா and இரா sit two syllables apart in line 3 and 4, the snake and the night together.

thinai_evidence.note: the snake-haunted grove and the night meeting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; she refuses the night meeting (இரவுக்குறி) for fear of the path

11.reading: The friend tells the lord of the mountain land, where the calf of a wild cow tramples with its hooves a honeycomb of sweet honey that has fallen under its weight, that if he keeps coming without marrying her, the girl of the rows of bangles will not live.
11.nuance: வரையக நாட and வரையால் play on one sound: lord of the hills (வரை), you who do not wed (வரை). The trampled honeycomb has been read as her ruined sweetness; it gives only one correspondence, a near miss for ullurai, and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the wild cow's calf and the fallen honeycomb of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; she presses him to marry

12.reading: The girl says she has embraced to the full, with longing, her bond with the lord of the forest land where flocks of curved-beaked parrots carry off the long ears of millet, and now the velan has firmly resolved to cut a goat kid.
12.nuance: The two halves are set side by side without comment: she knows the cause of her sickness, an embrace she chose, while the diviner the mother called readies a sacrifice for a god's seizure. The irony is all in the juxtaposition.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field raided by parrot flocks

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

13.reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord of the mountain land, where swarms of bees hum on the clustered kaanthal in a bower thick with the leaves of cool wild jasmine, has come at last, and their mother's harrying has gone away today.
13.nuance: அலையும் அலைபோயிற்று: the harrying itself has gone off, a play on அலை. The bees finding the kaanthal mirror his coming, but they carry a mood and are not tested as iraicchi. That he came to ask for her is inferred from the mother's anger ending.

thinai_evidence.note: kaanthal and wild jasmine of the hill bower

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse; his coming is taken as the coming to ask for her in marriage

14.reading: The girl says that because they say the lord of the land, where a stream carrying eaglewood from the clearing leaps over rocks and the waterfall from the sky brims in beauty, is a man of goodness, her shoulders have forgotten to waste even if he goes away.
14.nuance: The usual sign of separation, wasting shoulders, is cancelled by reputation: what others say of his goodness (என்பதனால்) is enough to keep her body whole. Her confidence in the bond, not the waiting, is the matter, so uri is taken as punarthal.

thinai_evidence.note: eaglewood and waterfall of the hill clearing

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the verse

links.note: Natrinai 57: while the herd of wild cows sleeps with their calves, a female monkey creeps up, squeezes the swollen udder and wrings the milk into her young one's hands. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 3: the monkey strokes the udder and the wild cow, glad as with her calf, lets the milk flow.
links.teaches: Held together they show one scene turned from theft to gift: the older poem's monkey steals while the cows sleep, fitting a friend who warns of the girl's ruin, while the later venba makes the cow consent, fitting a girl who says she cannot part, so the speaker's case decides whether the milk is stolen or given.

links.note: Kural 782: the friendship (கேண்மை) of the wise waxes like the crescent moon, that of fools wanes. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 4: the friendship of the worthy (சான்றவர் கேண்மை) stands firm and grows into strength, so the mountain lord's will too.
links.teaches: The venba lifts the Kural's maxim about friendship with the worthy into a girl's mouth as her proof that her lover will not fail, which shows the ethics books' rule of friendship being used, within the akam frame, to judge a lover's character before marriage.

links.note: Kural 1102: the man says the jewelled woman (அணியிழை) is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 5: the friend tells the man there is no medicine but him for the bright-jewelled girl (வயங்கிழை).
links.teaches: The same paradox of the lover as the only cure runs in both directions, the woman for the man in the Kural, the man for the woman here, and the change of speaker turns the Kural's private wonder into the friend's demand that he give the cure.

links.note: Akananuru 318: the friend tells the man who comes alone at night by a path made fearful by elephants, snakes and tigers not to come from today, and to blow his horn on reaching home so they know he is safe. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 10: the girl asks her friend to tell the lord of the snake-haunted groves not to come by night, to keep a life safe.
links.teaches: The long poem spells out what the four lines only hint, that refusing the night meeting is an act of care for the man's life on a dangerous path, and the venba moves the plea into the girl's own wish (குறையொன்று உடையேன்), showing the same refusal felt from inside.

links.note: Akananuru 242: the mother, not knowing of the man who chased parrots from the millet with them, calls the ignorant velan, and before the kid's life is given he should come and embrace the girl. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 12: parrots raid the millet, the girl has embraced him fully, and the velan has resolved to cut the kid.
links.teaches: Both set the embrace against the kid's sacrifice, but the older poem makes the embrace the remedy that must come before the rite, while the venba gives both as done, which leaves the velan preparing a useless sacrifice for a cure already taken.

links.note: Kural 1233: the shoulders that swelled on the day of union now announce loudly that he has gone. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 14: because he is said to be good, her shoulders have forgotten to waste even if he leaves.
links.teaches: On a plain reading the two make incompatible claims about the same sign: the Kural takes wasting shoulders as the body's certain witness to separation, while the venba says trust in the man's goodness can stop the body from giving that witness at all.

source_issues: No verse in this chapter has a colophon thurai; every thurai_akam speaker and addressee is inferred from the verse.
0: the invocation to the elephant god is in a different style from the kurinji venbas and is probably a later addition to the book.
2 line 2: குன்றன is unclear (குன்று அன்ன, 'like a hill', would need a tenor); line 4 தலையளி ஒன்றுமற்(று) ஒன்றும் அனைத்து does not construe cleanly, and the verse is marked uncertain.
6 line 3: முடைந்தாட is not a usual verb for bathing; perhaps முனைந்து ஆட, bathing with zeal.
7 lines 1 and 3: வெறிகமழ் தண் is repeated (தண்சுனை, தண்சோலை), which may be a copying error in one line.
8 line 4: நேர்வனை reads as a misprint for நேர்வளை, 'friend of fitting bangles'.
10 lines 1-2: whose life is meant by நிறையில்லா மன்னுயிர் (hers, without restraint, or his) is unclear; the verse is marked uncertain.
11 line 1: பிரைசங் is probably பிரசம் (honey or bees).
12 lines 1-2: வளைலாய is probably வளைவாய், curved beak; நீரால் தெளிதிகழ் does not construe clearly; the verse is marked uncertain.
